UN General Assembly resolutions are not binding sources of international law under Article 38 of the ICJ Statute. They are recommendations (UN Charter Arts. 10 and 13), so they are neither equivalent to treaties nor automatically customary law. They matter as evidence: they can help show state practice and *opinio juris* for customary law, as the ICJ found in *Nicaragua* (1986), but only when they reflect widespread and representative state support, and they are binding only on internal UN matters such as budget decisions. Neither option in the team note is correct, since "always customary law" and "equivalent to treaties" both overstate their status.

CONFIDENCE: 85
